title: Azerbaijan Denies Link to Espionage Case Involving Former German Spy Chief
content:
Azerbaijan has denied a report from a German magazine that claimed a former German spy chief — arrested Tuesday on treason and espionage charges — used classified state secrets to prepare an “analysis” for Baku’s intelligence services in exchange for money.

The denial follows a Tuesday statement from Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office announcing the arrest of August Hanning, who served as President of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005. Police also arrested his former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D.

Prosecutors accuse Hanning of procuring “nearly two thousand documents, many of which contained classified information,” with the help of Manfred D., in “exchange for payment,” from 2010 to 2022. While Hanning had by then retired from public service, Manfred D. worked as chief of staff for several subsequent BND heads from March 2012 to March 2026.

Hanning allegedly “commercially exploit[ed]” this classified information in his private consulting work. In one instance, prosecutors allege he used state secrets to draft an “analysis” for an unnamed foreign intelligence agency.

title: The Uzbek President’s Son-In-Law Secretly Acquired a UAE Passport While Serving as a Top Security Chief
content:
At the 2023 UN climate change conference in Dubai Otabek Umarov watched in the wings as his boss, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, met with his United Arab Emirates (UAE) counterpart.

Sporting a crisp navy suit and tie, Umarov at the time was the second most important official charged with protecting the Uzbek president. Perhaps more importantly, he was –– and remains –– married to Mirziyoyev’s youngest daughter, and is widely seen as an influential behind-the-scenes power broker.

But on that December day in Dubai, Umarov carried a potentially career-ending secret: seven months earlier, he had covertly obtained an Emirati passport requiring his sworn fealty to the state led by the man his father-in-law was talking to, President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Under UAE law, foreigners can only obtain citizenship through a nomination by a royal court or senior official, and requires swearing an oath of allegiance to the Emirates.

Uzbek military law governing the security post Umarov occupied at the time prohibited his second citizenship, and would have served as possible grounds for discharge from active duty.

title: Ex-Ukrainian Lawmaker Sent to Trial Over $1.3 Million Fraud Scheme
content:
Ukrainian anti-corruption authorities have sent a case to trial charging former lawmaker Heorhii Lohvynskyi and five others with misappropriating 54.18 million hryvnias (about $1.3 million) in state funds and laundering the proceeds.

Investigators allege that between 2013 and 2016, Lohvynskyi organized a scheme involving Golden Mandarin Oil LLC and a debt dispute with energy company Kyivenergo. The group allegedly used a fraudulent "friendly settlement" at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) to trick the Ukrainian government into paying off a private corporate debt with public money.

According to the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), a representative of Golden Mandarin Oil applied to the ECHR seeking payment from the state over a debt Kyivenergo allegedly owed under a 2009 domestic court ruling. Investigators say the company concealed from the ECHR that the legal right to claim the debt had already been transferred to a third party.

title: Montenegro Moves to Seize Vast Real Estate Empire of Fugitive Crime Boss
content:
Authorities in Montenegro might not be able to catch the country's most notorious fugitive crime boss, but they are moving to dismantle his financial empire.

The Special State Prosecutor's Office asked Tuesday the High Court in Podgorica to permanently confiscate a sprawling portfolio of real estate and luxury vehicles it believes is in his or his wife’s possession. While the official statement only identified the targets by their initials, R.Z. and his wife, T.Z., the request appears to be detailing the hidden wealth of the reputed Kavač clan leader Radoje Zvicer and his wife Tamara Zvicer. Local media reports also name the two as the targets of this request.

The timing of this massive forfeiture request is no coincidence. It serves as one of the first major tests of Montenegro's sweeping new "Anti-Mafia Law," passed on September 4. The government hailed the legislation as a "historic step" that has already caused an "earthquake in criminal circles," specifically because it empowers the state to permanently confiscate assets in organized crime cases even before a final judicial verdict is reached.
snippet: Authorities in Montenegro might not be able to catch the country's most notorious fugitive crime boss, but they are moving to dismantle his financial empire.

title: Cocaine Boatmen Are Being Blown Up By US Airstrikes, But The Drugs Keep Flowing From Colombia
content:
First, you hear the high-pitched whine of drones overhead. Next comes the boom of explosions.

“And then in the following days, the sea brings in a jerrycan, pieces of a boat, drugs, people too,” says Alberto, a local businessman living on the Colombian peninsula of La Guajira.

This grim sequence of events has become familiar for those based along this arid strip of desert, whose shores are lapped by a part of the Caribbean Sea that has been the site of some 20 deadly U.S. strikes on speedboats over the past year.

The U.S. military campaign against the alleged “narco-terrorists” manning these vessels, known as Operation Southern Spear, has faded from headline news since the first attack was launched over a year ago on September 2. 

Yet it continues to destroy small boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific — with at least 235 dead in some 70 strikes so far — in the face of heavy criticism from legal experts and rights groups, who call it an ineffective program of what are essentially extrajudicial murders.
snippet: First, you hear the high-pitched whine of drones overhead. Next comes the boom of explosions.

title: Prosecution of Tren de Aragua Accused Mastermind Deemed Complex Case
content:
A suspected cybercriminal who allegedly bankrolled the notorious Tren de Aragua gang through a multimillion-dollar ATM fraud scheme was arrested and will remain behind bars to face a complex prosecution in Nebraska, just days after the Venezuelan was blacklisted by the Treasury Department.

In a news conference Saturday in Omaha that began with, “well we got him,” FBI Special Agent in Charge Eugene Kowel said Anibal Alexander Canelón Aguirre, an alleged computer whiz and hacker tied to the transnational gang, was captured on the high seas.

During his news conference, Kowel said the FBI in Omaha received assistance from the U.S. Coast Guard and the FBI's Critical Incident Response Group. Canelón Aguirre, he said, was subsequently transported by sea and air to the District of Nebraska.

The FBI’s web page for its most-wanted fugitives now shows a red bar across his photo reading “Captured.”

However, Kowel’s account contrasts with statements made just weeks earlier by FBI Director Kash Patel. During a Senate hearing, Patel announced the fugitive’s capture in Venezuela without explicitly naming him or providing further details.

title: Leaked Video of Uruguayan Kingpin Triggers Mass Arrests Across Bolivian Justice System
content:
Even from inside an American prison cell, the Uruguayan drug kingpin Sebastián Marset managed to shatter the highest echelons of Bolivian justice this week.

The sudden release on Wednesday of two video recordings from Marset’s arrest in March sparked a sweeping law enforcement purge, leading to the detention of 14 high-ranking figures — including prosecutors, police commanders, the country’s attorney general, and the former national director of Bolivia’s special counter-narcotics unit.

The operation included raids on prosecutorial offices in Sucre, La Paz, and Santa Cruz after the newly surfaced video footage showed Marset claiming that the attorney general, Roger Mariaca, and other top law enforcement figures had shielded his criminal syndicate.

Bolivia’s Minister of Government, Marco Antonio Oviedo, described the operation as the dismantling of a “criminal organization entrenched in the justice system” that was dedicated to “protecting, encouraging, and supporting narco-terrorism.”

title: EU Froze Sierra Leone Aid for Harboring Alleged Drug Kingpin, Netherlands Says
content:
The European Commission has suspended nearly $20 million in aid to Sierra Leone’s 2026 budget due to the West African country’s harboring one of Europe's most wanted fugitives, alleged cocaine kingpin Joseph "Jos" Leijdekkers, Dutch Justice Minister David van Weel said Thursday.

Posting on social media from the EU’s Justice and Home Affairs Council meeting, van Weel wrote: “At the JHA Council meeting in Luxembourg, discussions are focusing on European security, the EU sanctions regime for organized crime. A positive development in this context is that the EU will no longer provide budget support to the authorities of Sierra Leone this year.”

Later in the day, he told Dutch public broadcaster NOS that the EU had suspended 18 million euro (roughly $20 million) in aid to Sierra Leone because the West African country is not cooperating with the Netherlands’ extradition request of Leijdekkers, a Dutch citizen.

Courts in the Netherlands and Belgium have handed Leijdekkers more than 100 years in prison sentences in absentia in convictions for a range of crimes, including drug trafficking, assault, armed robbery, and attempted murder.

title: Amnesty Report Documents Morocco's Sustained Spyware Campaign Against Civil Society
content:
Amnesty International has released a new report showing how, despite official denials, Moroccan authorities used surveillance spyware against civil society between 2017 and 2021, and possibly continued to use it later. 

The rights watchdog’s report, titled “We start with the verdict”: Inside Morocco’s surveillance machine, details how the government deployed Israeli firm NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware to target civil society figures both domestically and abroad in what Amnesty described as “unlawful surveillance attacks.”

“The report presents extensive technical and forensic evidence confirming the DGST acquisition of Pegasus, confirms that civil society members were the primary target of Morocco from the very beginning of their Pegasus use in 2017,” Donncha Ó Cearbhaill, leader of the Security Lab told OCCRP.

According to the findings, the government's deployment of Pegasus evolved in tandem with the technological development in the spyware. Amnesty documented the use of sophisticated attack vectors, ranging from “one-click” phishing links requiring user interaction to advanced “zero-click” exploits capable of compromising devices without any action from the target.

title: U.K. Sanctions Four Georgians Over Occupied Ukraine Visit
content:
The U.K. has sanctioned four Georgians—including the brother-in-law of Tbilisi’s mayor—for “legitimising Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territory” after they met with the head of a Russian-backed separatist republic.

The designations are part of a broader British sanctions package announced in response to intensifying Russian drone strikes against Ukraine in September. According to a press release Thursday, the wider measures target Russia’s “shadow fleet,” Kremlin propagandists, and individuals allegedly involved in human rights abuses against Ukrainian civilians. 

“The U.K. will not flinch in our support for Ukraine,” said Europe Minister Lord Wood of Anfield.

The U.K. sanctions notice states the four men “joined a delegation of Georgian politicians who met with the head of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic, and subsequently publicised the visit.” All four now face U.K. asset freezes and travel bans.

The sanctioned delegates include political commentator Paata Abuladze, Mamuka Pipia, leader of the minor Solidarity for Peace party, party member Giorgi Iremadze, and Nikoloz Mzhavanadze, founder of a Georgian Russian-language TV channel.

title: Ex-Hungarian Minister Detained in $53 Million Graft Probe
content:
Black-masked law enforcement officers escorted Balázs Hankó, a former Hungarian culture minister, into a district court on Thursday, where a judge ordered him held in pretrial detention over allegations that he masterminded the widespread misappropriation of state funds to benefit the party of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.

Hankó was taken into custody after Hungary's Parliament voted 139 to 0 on Monday to strip his legislative immunity. Before surrendering to prosecutors later that evening, he spent the day inside the Parliament building surrounded by his family, framing his pending arrest as political persecution.

"My conscience is clear; this is a political show trial," Hankó said in a video broadcast live on Orbán’s Facebook page before walking out alongside relatives and lawmakers from Fidesz, Orbán's right-wing party, which is now in opposition.

title: Raids Across Europe Target Far-Right Network Accused of Producing Neo-Nazi Music
content:
Authorities in five European countries carried out coordinated searches on Wednesday as part of an investigation into a suspected far-right criminal organization accused of producing and selling sound recordings containing music that incited hatred and spread National Socialist, antisemitic, racist and dehumanizing ideology.

The Rostock Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania State Office of Criminal Investigation said four suspects, aged 55, 52, 48 and 43, are being investigated for alleged membership in a criminal organization. One of them is also suspected of acting as its ringleader. The searches were carried out under warrants issued by an investigating judge at the Rostock Local Court.

Investigators suspect the four formed a permanent association no later than 2020 and worked together in an organized division of labor to produce and sell recordings containing hate-inciting music.

title: Leaked Warrant List Reveals How Turkmenistan Targets Critics Abroad
content:
Even as he bounced between Poland, Sweden and the Netherlands seeking political asylum, Nurmuhammet Annayev kept pressure on the authoritarian regime in his home country of Turkmenistan.

Annayev runs a YouTube channel that has brought him popularity among fellow critics of the Turkmenistan government. But his activism has also kept him firmly in the regime’s sights.

“Turns out they can even take people from abroad,” he said. “These guys are ready to eliminate — to disappear — the person standing in front of them to achieve their goals.”

Annayev, whose exact location OCCRP is not disclosing due to security reasons, is right to believe he is a target of Turkmenistan’s sprawling security and legal apparatus. 

OCCRP’s member center, Turkmen.news, has obtained an arrest warrant list from the Ministry of Internal Affairs showing that Annayev was wanted in his home country for political reasons. He was accused of “calls for an armed seizure of power or change of the constitutional order,” as well as “open calls for extremist activities.”

title: The US Blacklists Alleged Venezuelan Cyber Crime Mastermind
content:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury on Wednesday announced it had placed on a special blacklist Aníbal Alexander Canelón Aguirre— a Venezuelan who appears on the FBI’s "Ten Most Wanted" list—identifying him as a key link in a financial network for the notorious crime group Tren de Aragua. 

Canelón Aguirre is wanted by the Justice Department for allegedly leading a multi-million dollar ATM fraud scheme. Authorities accuse him of masterminding a jackpotting operation involving malware that when installed allows thieves to direct the bank machine to spew out money.

The alleged Venezuelan hacker topped a list of six Venezuelans and three Mexicans whose names were announced Wednesday as having been added to a group of specially designated nationals. It effectively locks them out of the global financial system. Six of the named are co-defendants of Canelón Aguirre in a U.S. prosecution.

The accused hacker has been on the run, lending his tech skills to the likes of a Romanian mafia operating along Mexico's white-sand beaches and became the cyber "engineer" of the infamous Venezuelan Tren de Aragua gang.

title: Fiji Overhauls Evidence Security After 52 Kilos of Cocaine Vanish from Court
content:
Fiji’s police chief has ordered the immediate transfer of all illicit drugs and cash to highly secure police vaults after officials confirmed Wednesday that 52.4 kilograms of cocaine tied to two major criminal cases were stolen from a High Court evidence room, in the capital, Suva, with much of the contraband replaced by flour.

The incident is seen as a significant blow to a police force already struggling with corruption allegations amid a surge in international drug trafficking. However, Police Commissioner Rusiate Tudravu maintained that police are not responsible for guarding evidence once it is transferred to the judiciary, comparing the nation’s High Court to a private residence.

“It’s just like your home,” he told an OCCRP reporter. “You’re the boss of your home. I cannot come and tell you I’ll guard your home. Simple.”

Fiji, a nation of fewer than a million people, is facing an escalating drug crisis. It has become a transit hub for cocaine smuggled from South America to Australia and New Zealand, and is now seeing a spike in domestic use driving soaring HIV rates linked to intravenous methamphetamine use.

title: Egyptian Security Services Arrest Entire Newsroom within 24 Hours
content:
Egyptian security services have arrested six journalists between Monday and Tuesday, all working for local independent investigative journalism platform Matsadaash. According to a statement published by the news platform on Wednesday, the crackdown began with raids on the homes of two of the journalists on Monday evening and early Tuesday morning. Over the following hours, authorities raided the homes of the other journalists working for the platform, without providing “any clear explanation for this escalation or its legal basis,” the statement said.

“With these latest arrests, the entire editorial team in the Matsadaash newsroom is now in detention.”  

In a separate statement, the journalists’ legal representative, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, said that all six journalists' whereabouts remain unknown, adding that they have not been allowed to contact their families or legal team.

title: Dutch Police Arrest Alleged Member of Hacking Group that Targeted FBI
content:
Dutch Police have announced the arrest of a 24-year-old alleged member of the cybercrime group ShinyHunters that has been responsible for a string of major data breaches, including the hacking of an FBI website last week.

In a statement Tuesday, police said that following the suspect's arrest last week that they found information on his laptop revealing that he was arranging two murders abroad. Police added that this alleged plot “is not related to the investigation into ShinyHunters.” The statement did not disclose the suspect's name. 

Addressing the ShinyHunters group directly in a video statement, , FBI's Cyber Division Assistant Director Brett Leatherman urged the hacking group to surrender to authorities. “To the remaining members of ShinyHunters: You’ve heard about the arrest of your colleague,” Leatherman said.

title: EPPO Indicts Two Polish Nationals in €100 Million Electronics VAT Fraud Scheme
content:
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) in Katowice has indicted two Polish nationals alleging that they were part of a cross-border VAT fraud and money laundering scheme involving more than 100 million euros ($113.58 million) in fraudulent invoices. The indictment is the first to stem from "Operation Escape Room," a broader investigation targeting an electronic device trading ring operating across Austria, Belgium, Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands, and Poland.

According to prosecutors, the network used hundreds of shell companies and fake invoices to conceal transactions, evade VAT, and claim illegal tax reimbursements. In addition to the fraudulent invoices in Poland, the scheme caused an estimated 47 million euros ($53.39 million) in unpaid VAT damage in Belgium and 22 million euros ($24.99 million) in the Netherlands. If convicted, the defendants face between seven and a half and 25 years in prison.

title: Trafigura Bought Venezuelan Gold in ‘Historic’ US Deal in March. It’s Still in Storage.
content:
Six months after the U.S. government announced it would begin gold imports from Venezuela following years of sanctions prevented the trade, the first major tranche of gold from the deal is still in storage, OCCRP has learned.

The gold is being held by commodities-trading giant Trafigura, which became the first international firm to take advantage of relaxed U.S. restrictions on purchasing Venezuelan gold in March, in what the White House touted as a “historic” deal.

"All gold Trafigura has purchased from Venezuela to-date is currently in storage, under Trafigura's control,” a Trafigura spokesperson told OCCRP in early September.

The firm declined to comment on why the gold had not been sold yet in the U.S., but experts said the hold-up could be related to supply-chain issues. Venezuelan gold is extracted from a lawless and violent region, and it may be difficult to meet U.S. requirements to show it has been produced ethically.

title: Iraqi Lawmaker Sentenced to 7 Years, Fined $21 Million for Illicit Enrichment
content:
An Iraqi court has sentenced sitting lawmaker Mohammed Farman Shaher to seven years in prison for illicit enrichment, ordering him to pay the equivalent of over $21.4 million in restitution and fines, according to legal authorities.

Shaher was ordered to repay 11.8 billion Iraqi dinars ($9.01 million) and $1.73 million in illicit gains, alongside an equivalent fine.

Shaher, who was arrested on June 28, serves on parliament’s Oil and Gas Committee. He is a member of the Sunni Taqaddum Party, led by former parliament speaker Mohammed al-Halbousi and home to current speaker Haibat al-Halbousi.

title: Seven Arrested in Massive EU Fraud Scheme Selling Used Phones as New
content:
An international law enforcement operation led by the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) resulted in the arrests of seven people, including two alleged ringleaders, to dismantle a criminal network suspected of selling more than one million used mobile phones as new, the EPPO announced Tuesday. The cross-border crackdown, code-named "Troja," involved more than 1,700 officers conducting over 160 searches across 19 countries. Authorities estimate the scheme defrauded European Union consumers of at least 300 million euros ($340 million) and caused 30 million euros ($34 million) in value-added tax (VAT) losses.

According to prosecutors, the syndicate assembled phones from used components in Hong Kong and the United Arab Emirates. The devices were then shipped through the Netherlands to warehouses in Germany, where they were cleaned, packaged, and sold on online marketplaces to unsuspecting customers across the EU as brand-new products.

title: Lithuanian Mayor Found Guilty in Expense Fraud Case
content:
A Lithuanian court has found Prienai district Mayor Alvydas Vaicekauskas guilty of abuse of office, fraud, and document forgery over false expense claims he submitted while serving as a municipal councilor. The Alytus District Court fined him 7,500 euros ($8,800) and barred him for three years from holding elected or appointed public office once the judgment becomes final.

Investigators found that between 2019 and 2023 Vaicekauskas submitted 17 expense reports containing false information about fuel purchases purportedly related to his council work, in some cases using bank cards belonging to other people. Prosecutors said he improperly obtained about 1,113 euros from the municipality.

The ruling can be appealed within 20 days. His lawyer, Audrius Pėstininkas, told OCCRP the defense would appeal the verdict. “We did not find in the judgment answers to the questions raised by the defense, and naturally we still do not understand which legal act or procedure A. Vaicekauskas violated, or where the court saw document forgery or deception in his actions,” he said.

title: OCCRP Partner Siraj Wins 2026 Samir Kassir Award
content:
The Samir Kassir Award for Freedom of the Press has named Ali Al-Ibrahim, co-director of OCCRP member center Siraj, and Syrian investigative journalist Mais Katt as joint winners in its investigative reporting category. The award recognizes  their September 2025 cross-border investigative project, “Syria’s Stolen Children: How the Assad Regime Turned Detainees’ Children into Hostages Between Intelligence Agencies and Orphanages.” 

Published a year ago following the fall of Bashar al-Assad in late 2024, the investigation documents how officials from al-Assad’s security services abducted hundreds of Syrian children of political detainees and hid them inside children’s charities in order to coerce and intimidate their families. The investigation exposed the complicity of several care institutions, including facilities run by the major European charity SOS Children’s Villages, whose leadership knew about the abuses for years and remained silent.

The Samir Kassir Award, which has been presented by the E.U. since 2006, selected the investigation from 194 submissions across 11 countries in North Africa, the Middle East and the Gulf.

title: French Prosecutors Seek Prison Time for Ex-Minister Dati in Renault-Nissan Case
content:
France's former Minister of Justice and Minister of Culture, Rachida Dati, faces a requested four-year sentence for allegations of corruption and influence peddling stemming from her alleged lobbying work for the Renault-Nissan carmaking group between 2009 and 2013, OCCRP media partner Le Monde reports.

Almost a week after the opening of her trial in Paris, French prosecutors on Monday requested a four-year prison sentence for Dati, who currently serves as the mayor of a Paris arrondissement, with two years suspended and two years of house arrest. Prosecutors accuse Dati of receiving 900,000 euros (over $1 million) for providing consulting services to a Dutch subsidiary of Renault-Nissan without actually performing any work, all while serving as a Member of the European Parliament and working as an attorney.

Prosecutors also sought a four-year jail term for co-defendant Carlos Ghosn, the former CEO of Renault-Nissan who is being tried in absentia over charges including abuse of corporate assets, breach of trust, corruption, and active trading in influence.

title: Wife, Daughter of Suspected Ecuador Gang Boss Arrested in Colombia
content:
Colombian authorities arrested two Ecuadorian women suspected of helping manage the finances of a major transnational criminal organization, Ecuadorian police said Sunday. The women were detained in Sabana de Torres during a joint operation involving police from both nations, Colombia’s GAULA anti-kidnapping unit and the FBI. Ecuadorian authorities described both women as high-value targets and said they are believed to be the wife and daughter of the alleged crime boss José Adolfo Macías Villamar, known as “Fito.”

Macías formerly led Los Choneros, an Ecuador-based criminal organization involved in cocaine trafficking, firearms trafficking and violent crime. He was recaptured in Ecuador in June 2025 and extradited to the United States the following month, where he faces federal drug and firearms charges. Ecuadorian prosecutors have separately investigated alleged money laundering involving his family circle, saying suspicious transactions worth more than $2 million entered the country’s financial system between 2016 and 2023.

title: Internal Watchdog says Data Leaks and Bribery Push French Police Misconduct Cases to Five-Year High
content:
Offenses involving corruption, influence peddling, and other integrity violations within the French National Police surged by 45 percent between 2024 and 2025, reaching their highest level in five years, according to an internal oversight report released this week. 

The annual assessment by the General Inspectorate of the National Police, or IGPN, recorded 341 integrity breaches in 2025, up from 234 the previous year. The infractions encompassed bribery, conflicts of interest, embezzlement of public funds, extortion, breaches of professional secrecy, and the unauthorized handling of sensitive personal data.

The oversight agency reported steep increases across three primary categories: unauthorized queries of police databases, which jumped by 80 percent; corruption offenses, which rose by 33 percent; and breaches of professional secrecy, which increased by 25 percent.

Stéphane Hardouin, the head of the IGPN, acknowledged the sharp rise in misconduct. “There was a significant increase in breaches of integrity,” Hardouin said, pointing specifically to the rise in corruption and database misuse.

title: Guns, Camouflage, and Facebook: How Colombia’s Biggest ‘Narcoinfluencer’ Weaponized Social Media
content:
Nain Pérez had all the qualities a Gen-Z influencer could ask for. 

With an easy smile and thick black hair cut into a stylish hi-top fade, the 27-year-old Colombian built a huge following on Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok by sharing eye-catching images of a high-flying lifestyle: fast motorcycles, big cars, and a beautiful girlfriend known as “Bebecita.”

But behind the romantic snapshots and aspirational memes was a darker reality: Pérez, who went by the alias Bendito Menor (“Little Blessing”), also openly broadcast his role as a rising member of the Self-Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada, an illegal armed group better known by its Spanish abbreviation ACSN. 

Although he wasn’t the most powerful member of the ACSN — one of several armed groups in Colombia that profit from crimes like drug trafficking and extortion — he was easily the most famous, with a huge fan base that hung on his every move.

title: Bosnian Police Officer Dies by Suicide Following Raid
content:
A Bosnian police officer died by suicide Wednesday after authorities searched his office during a multi-city anti-trafficking operation, officials and local media reported. The State Investigation and Protection Agency (SIPA) stated Thursday the suspect suffered a self-inflicted gunshot wound during raids across Sarajevo, Doboj, and Bratunac targeting an organized crime network involved in arms and drug trafficking.

Local investigative outlet Istraga identified the suspect as a Sarajevo Canton police officer who shot himself inside the Ilijaš police station following the search, saying he was allegedly tied to the notorious Swedish criminal ring known as Foxtrot. According to Istraga, the operation was coordinated with Europol to target a ring allegedly supplying weapons to the gang led by Majid Rawa. Local media also linked the operation to last week's record bust in the same municipality.

During the operation, SIPA said officers seized nine hunting rifles, five pistols, about 190 rounds of ammunition, and forged documents allegedly used to fraudulently issue firearms permits and facilitate illegal weapons sales.

title: Former Anti-Corruption Official Among Two Iraqi Lawmakers Jailed for Illicit Enrichment
content:
Iraq's Central Anti-Corruption Criminal Court has sentenced two lawmakers to seven years in prison each for illicit enrichment, tying their hidden wealth to an ongoing corruption probe into a senior oil official.

Alia Nassif Jassem Aziz Al Obaidi, known as Alia Nassif, an MP representing Baghdad who built a public profile on anti-corruption rhetoric, previously served as the first vice-chair of parliament’s Integrity Committee. She was transferred to the Finance Committee earlier this year and arrested on corruption charges on June 28, according to Iraq’s official news agency.

MP Ashwaq Salem Hassan has also been linked to the same corruption probe.

The current chairman of the Integrity Committee, Taha Al-Difai, told OCCRP that the sentences were based on the interrogation of detained Deputy Oil Minister Adnan al-Jumaili by an investigating judge. According to Al-Difai, al-Jumaili admitted to having illicit dealings with the two lawmakers.

Investigators subsequently uncovered unexplained cash and real estate wealth that neither woman had reported on their mandatory financial disclosures, which officials must file within three months of taking office.

title: US Charges Tech CEO, Russian Over Hidden Ownership
content:
U.S. authorities have charged the CEO of a digital forensics company and a Russian national with allegedly concealing the firm's Russian ownership and the origins of software sold to U.S. government agencies, including the Secret Service.

Lee Reiber, 55, CEO of Virginia-based Oxygen Forensics, and Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov, 52, of Moscow, were charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, the U.S. Justice Department announced Wednesday. Reiber was arrested in Idaho on Sunday and later released on bond. Davydov was detained the same day at London's Heathrow Airport before boarding a flight to Istanbul, and the United States plans to seek his extradition.

Prosecutors allege that Oxygen Forensics portrayed itself to U.S. government customers as an independent American company, while Davydov and four other Russian nationals actually owned and controlled it through a Cyprus-based holding company.

title: Vanuatu Denies Revoking Andrew Tate’s Citizenship
content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Vanuatu has denied a media report that it had revoked the citizenship of online influencer and alleged rapist Andrew Tate.

The denial comes after the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) reported on Monday that the self-described misogynist had been stripped of his Vanuatu passport, which OCCRP revealed last year had been granted in 2022 under the country’s citizenship-by-investment program.

The chairman of Vanuatu’s citizenship commission, Charlie Maniel, told OCCRP the commission had never made a decision to revoke Tate’s citizenship.

In a statement forwarded to OCCRP by Maniel, the commission said Tate’s citizenship was not revoked because he had not been convicted of a crime. Vanuatu law allows for citizenship to be revoked if someone is sentenced to 10 years or more in prison, the statement said.

“The Commission was informed of [the charges against Tate]; however, it has not made a decision to revoke the grant of citizenship, as there is currently insufficient evidence to support such action based on the Citizenship Office’s records and the recent due diligence information received,” the statement said.
snippet: The government of the Pacific island nation of Vanuatu has denied a media report that it had revoked the citizenship of online influencer and alleged rapist Andrew Tate.

title: Federal Judge Weighs Limits of U.S. Reach in Trial of Accused Kingpin Sebastián Marset
content:
A federal judge will decide by Nov. 6 whether to dismiss criminal charges against Sebastián Marset, the self-proclaimed South American drug lord whose defense attorney conceded in court on Wednesday that while his client is a drug trafficker, his illicit empire fell entirely outside United States jurisdiction.

During a detailed two-hour evidentiary hearing in federal district court in Alexandria, Judge Rossie D. Alston Jr. weighed a number of defense motions seeking to dismantle the federal indictment against Marset, ranging from jurisdictional challenges to allegations of improper interrogations and vindictive prosecution.

The allegation of vindication prosecution didn’t sit well with Alston, who called it a “very serious” allegation and noted he personally had presided over cases involving the prosecutors, for whom he had high regard.

Defense attorney Robert Feitel quickly interjected that he wasn’t referencing individuals but the process by which Marset was captured in Bolivia, sent to the United States and interrogated without lawyers present. He sought to discredit Michael Greisen, one of the lead agents for the Drug Enforcement Administration in its efforts to capture Marset.

title: Azerbaijan Pardons French Citizen as EU Lifts Sanctions on Russian Billionaire
content:
President Ilham Aliyev of Azerbaijan pardoned 20 prisoners on Wednesday, including a French national jailed on espionage charges, shortly after the European Union removed Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov from its sanctions list.

Among those granted clemency under Aliyev’s decree was Martin Ryan, a French citizen arrested in late 2023 and sentenced by an Azerbaijani court in March to 10 years in prison.

The pardons followed a broader diplomatic deal struck after France lobbied for Usmanov's delisting. The E.U. Council announced Tuesday that it had also lifted sanctions against Mikhail Fridman, a Russia-connected businessman, while extending restrictions—including travel bans and asset freezes—on roughly 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years in response to the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine.

title: EPPO Arrests Suspect in $79M Cross-Border VAT Fraud Probe
content:
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office has arrested another suspect in its “Escape Room” investigation into a cross-border VAT carousel fraud network operating across six EU countries. 

The wider network allegedly used hundreds of shell companies and fictitious invoices to conceal transactions involving electronic devices and evade VAT in Austria, Belgium, Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands and Poland. EPPO estimates the scheme caused at least $79 million in losses in the Netherlands and Belgium. Eight other suspects were arrested in Belgium, the Netherlands and Poland in October 2025. 

Prosecutors allege the arrested man acted as a broker between companies in the scheme, improperly claimed VAT refunds and continued the operation through new companies after authorities raided the network in 2025. His activities alone may have caused about $4.6 million in losses, while authorities seized around $4 million in real estate, a car, stock, receivables and bank accounts.
snippet: The European Public Prosecutor’s Office has arrested another suspect in its “Escape Room” investigation into a cross-border VAT carousel fraud network operating across six EU countries.

title: Human Trafficking Raid Exposes Suspected Cyber Scam Operation in Papua New Guinea
content:
Papua New Guinea police rescued 39 Indonesians believed to have been trafficked to work in a cyber scam compound, the first case of its kind uncovered in the Pacific island nation.

Four Chinese nationals were also detained in connection with the Tuesday raid in the country’s capital, Port Moresby, PNG police Commissioner David Manning told OCCRP.

“What we did find in there was 39 Indonesian citizens, 34 that were male and five females, all adults but they’ve been in very cramped, very cramped conditions,” Manning said.

Manning also said police seized a large number of documents and electronic devices from the property, a house in Port Moresby’s inner suburbs. He said the incident was the first case he was aware of involving the suspected trafficking of foreign nationals into the country to carry out online fraud.

He added that as far as he is aware Papua New Guinea was the final destination for the suspected trafficking victims.

“All indications are they were brought in specifically to run this scam from Papua New Guinea,” he said.
snippet: Papua New Guinea police rescued 39 Indonesians believed to have been trafficked to work in a cyber scam compound, the first case of its kind uncovered in the Pacific island nation.

title: Former Mother-In-Law of Dismissed Ukraine Prosecutor General Denies Buying Dubai Villa
content:
With a cloud of controversy hanging over former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko — who was dismissed last week after his office was raided by anti-corruption officers — information has now emerged about a mystery villa in Dubai.

Records show Kravchenko’s former mother in law was listed as the owner of the Dubai villa. But she denies making the purchase.

Alina Shkrobanets acquired villa for about $670,000 in 2023, according to leaked Dubai property data obtained by OCCRP and shared with Schemes, the investigative unit of RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service.

At the time, Kravchenko headed the Kyiv Regional Military Administration and was married to Alina Shkrobanets' daughter, Olena.

“I didn’t buy anything in the United Arab Emirates,” Alina Shkrobanets told Schemes, suggesting her identity details might have been used without her knowledge.

“I’m wondering if someone might have used my information against me,” she said in a phone interview.

title: Albanian Court Orders House Arrest for Intelligence Chief
content:
An Albanian court has ordered the director of the State Intelligence Service (SHISH), Vlora Hyseni, to be put under house arrest and suspended from public duty as part of a sweeping investigation into public tender fraud, the Special Prosecutor’s Office (SPAK) announced Tuesday. The development prompted Prime Minister Edi Rama to announce her immediate removal from office.

The Special Court against Corruption and Organized Crime (GJKKO) approved the security measures at the request of SPAK. Prosecutors are investigating Hyseni for allegedly assisting a perpetrator of a criminal offense and disclosing state secrets.

However, the house arrest order could not be immediately executed because Hyseni was in Baku, Azerbaijan, attending an international conference of intelligence service heads when officers searched her apartment.

Speaking from New York, Prime Minister Edi Rama said Hyseni’s dismissal is immediate and that he will consult President Bajram Begaj to appoint a successor, emphasizing that the court must determine her guilt or innocence independently.

title: Romanian Ex-Presidential Candidate Held in €1.1M Fraud Case
content:
Romanian prosecutors have asked a Bucharest court to place former presidential candidate Călin Georgescu and businessman Ionel Rusen in pretrial detention for 30 days over an alleged organized criminal group and a 1.1 million euro ($1.26 million) fraud. 

According to a prosecution filing reviewed by OCCRP, investigators allege Georgescu, Rusen and Italian businessman Massimiliano Arena persuaded a Romanian businessman to transfer money as a guarantee for a foreign credit line that never materialized. Prosecutors say Georgescu initiated the arrangement and introduced Rusen as someone capable of securing the financing.

The victim first transferred 1 million euros and later another 100,000 euros after being told the loan could be increased from six million euros to 15 million, the filing says. Prosecutors detained Georgescu and Rusen for 24 hours following searches that uncovered electronic devices, signal jammers and documents suspected of being false. The filing also cites secretly recorded conversations in which Georgescu discussed buying property in Italy and seeking political asylum, which prosecutors cited in arguing that he posed a flight risk.

title: Disappearance of 2 Journalists in Djibouti Raises Concerns for Their Safety
content:
The Committee to Protect Journalists said Sunday that it is “deeply concerned” by reports that South African investigative journalist Micah Reddy and local fixer Kooki Mahmoud have gone missing in Djibouti, and urged authorities “to immediately clarify their whereabouts and ensure their safety.”

Contact with Reddy, the African coordinator for the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), and Mahmoud, a Djibouti-based journalist, was lost Saturday at approximately 1 p.m. local time, said an ICIJ statement. The statement, issued Sunday, said ICIJ is gravely concerned for their safety and authorities in Djibouti have not so far responded to its requests for information.

“We are calling on the government of Djibouti to: Immediately clarify Reddy and Mahmoud's whereabouts and confirm their well-being; Launch a prompt, transparent investigation into their disappearance; Keep their families, colleagues and employers fully and promptly informed,” the ICIJ statement said.

title: Bosnia Seizes 1.1 Tons of Synthetic Drugs Worth Up to €33 Million
content:
Authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina have seized nearly 1.1 metric tonnes of dangerous synthetic cathinones with a potential street value of up to 33 million euros ($37.82 million), and arrested two suspects, marking the largest synthetic drug bust in the history of the nation of roughly 3.5 million people, the State Border Service announced.

The seized substance—an extremely dangerous stimulant used as a substitute for cocaine and ecstasy—carries a wholesale market value of 5 million euros ($5.73 million), but its street value skyrockets when broken down into individual grams sold at 20 to 30 euros ($23 to $34.50) each across the region, according to the Border Police. In addition to the massive drug cache, officers confiscated a firearm, mobile phones, corporate documentation, official stamps, and specialized full-face respirator masks with advanced air-filtration systems used to protect operators during chemical synthesis and drug "cooking." The Border Police noted that investigators have not yet established the origin or final destination of the shipment, as the investigation remains ongoing.

title: Iraq Sentences Former Electricity Director General to Seven Years for illicit enrichment
content:
An Iraqi anti-corruption court has sentenced the former director general of a state electricity distribution firm to seven years in prison for illicit enrichment, ordering him to forfeit nearly $20 million in restitution and fines as part of a sweeping crackdown on graft in the country’s power sector.

The official, Alaa Samir Rashid Shukr Al-Jubouri, who headed the state-owned General Company of Electricity Distribution (Middle Region), was convicted by Iraq’s Central Criminal Court for Combating Corruption. According to the country’s Integrity Commission, Rashid amassed unexplained wealth exceeding 5.5 billion Iraqi dinars (about $4.2 million) along with an additional $5.5 million in U.S. currency.

The court ordered Rashid to return the illicit gains and levied an equivalent fine, bringing his total financial liability to approximately $19.4 million. Judges also upheld a freeze on his movable and immovable assets, paving the way for seizure.

title: Georgia Court Sentences Ex-Security Chief to 13 Years in Prison in Corruption Case
content:
The former head of the State Security Service of Georgia was found guilty this week of accepting more than $2 million in bribes and sentenced to 13 years in prison, as a corruption crackdown continues against former senior officials from the ruling Georgian Dream party. 

Grigol Liluashvili, who headed the security service from 2019 until 2025, was arrested last December following raids on his home and those of two other former ruling party elites.

Tbilisi City Court Judge Nino Tarashvili on Wednesday found Liluashvili guilty of “accepting bribes on an especially large scale,” said the Prosecutor's Office of Georgia’s press release announcing the verdict. 

Liluashvili’s lawyer Lana Tsertsvadze reacted outside the courtroom, telling reporters it was an “unjust verdict” that she would appeal.

“The defense and Mr. Grigol Liluashvili anticipated an acquittal because there was not a single piece of evidence in the case to prove his guilt,” Tsertsvadze said in a video interview. “Mr. Grigol Liluashvili will seek to establish his innocence through legal avenues. This unfounded, unlawful, and unjust decision will be challenged in the Court of Appeals.”
snippet: The former head of the State Security Service of Georgia was found guilty this week of accepting more than $2 million in bribes and sentenced to 13 years in prison, as a corruption crackdown continues

title: Six Convicted, €300M Confiscation Ordered in Mafia-Linked EU Tax Fraud
content:
A Milan court has sentenced six individuals to prison and ordered the confiscation of more than 300 million euros ($344.66 million) for their roles in a transnational tax fraud and money laundering syndicate tied to the Italian mafia, the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) announced on Thursday.

The convictions mark the latest judicial actions in "Operation Moby Dick," a massive EPPO investigation into a VAT carousel fraud scheme. Between 2020 and 2023, the network issued over 1.3 billion euros ($1.49 billion) in fake invoices for AirPods, laptops, and other electronics, resulting in 520 million euros ($597.35 million) in losses to EU and national budgets.

The Milan judge confirmed aggravated circumstances for the criminal syndicate’s aiding and abetting of a mafia association. According to the EPPO, one of the convicted defendants received illicit funds from a Camorra clan—which investigators previously linked to the Nuvoletta and Di Lauro groups—and funneled the money into the scheme to launder the mafia's proceeds.

title: Former Maduro Ally Pleads Guilty in US to $195M Money Laundering Scheme
content:
A Miami federal court brought a decade of investigative reporting to a close on Wednesday as Colombian-born businessman Alex Saab pleaded guilty to money laundering—years after Venezuelan news outlet Armando.info first began uncovering his state corruption schemes.

Saab, a top financial ally of ousted Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro, admitted to using the U.S. financial system to launder bribes connected to Venezuela’s Local Committees for Supply and Production (CLAP)—a state program meant to distribute food to impoverished communities. He faces up to 20 years in federal prison and has agreed to forfeit $195 million, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

The guilty plea serves as a vindication for Armando.info, a local investigative news outlet and OCCRP member center. More than  nine years ago, the outlet pioneered reporting that brought Saab out of the shadows, exposing his ties to multimillion-dollar state contracts and the delivery of low-quality food to vulnerable populations.

At the time, Saab and the Maduro government vehemently denied the links. Saab sued the Armando.info team in Venezuela, arguing he had no connection to the CLAP program.

title: Belgian Court Rules Treasury Lacked Authority to Reject Release of Russian Assets
content:
Belgium’s supreme administrative court has ruled that a decision by the country’s treasury department refusing to release frozen Russian assets was illegal.

The court, known as the Council of State, ruled that the Administrator General of the Treasury lacked the proper legal competence to determine whether or not to release the assets.

The September 11 ruling was first reported by De Tijd on Wednesday, and shared with OCCRP. 

The case originates from a request submitted by Russia’s BCS Bank in January 2023 to unfreeze its securities and cash, which had been blocked at Brussels-based securities manager Euroclear. 

The assets were frozen following E.U. sanctions imposed in 2022 on Moscow's main securities holder, the National Settlement Depository, in response to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

In July 2024, the Belgian treasury rejected BCS Bank’s request to unfreeze its securities and cash. The treasury alleged that the lender had failed to prove it had fully severed ties with Russia’s National Settlement Depository.

The Council of State ruling does not necessarily mean the frozen funds will be released.

title: Hackers Demand $3M Ransom in Revolut Data Leak
content:
A group claiming responsibility for a recent Revolut data breach has demanded 6,000 Monero—an untraceable, privacy-focused cryptocurrency—worth about $3 million, threatening to sell sensitive information belonging to hundreds of the fintech company’s customers if it is not paid within 24 hours.

The group, calling itself “iamnotavillain,” posted the ultimatum on its website on Wednesday alongside a countdown clock. It threatened to sell the information to other criminal groups if Revolut failed to pay.

A Revolut spokesperson told Reuters late Wednesday that the company had received no direct contact or ransom demand from the people claiming responsibility for the breach, and that there had been no negotiations with them.

The company first confirmed the breach on September 12, saying an unauthorized party had submitted fraudulent requests for customer information using an email account on the legitimate domain of a government agency. Revolut said its own systems and customer funds were not compromised and that it blocked the address after discovering the fraud.

title: Citizen Lab: Israeli Firm May Have Run Angola Influence Campaign
content:
Israeli influence-for-hire company BlackCore appears to have trained members of an Angolan government communications team and helped them run a covert social media campaign, according to research by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab.

Citizen Lab examined websites and other online infrastructure linked to BlackCore and obtained what researchers identified as the company’s final report on a training program in Angola. One BlackCore webpage, titled “Angolan Government Campaign,” advertised training in storytelling, copywriting, traffic management and social media operations. It also described plans to launch live campaigns on Meta and TikTok.

The final report said the program began on January 19, 2026, and continued for more than 14 weeks, ending sometime in April. BlackCore described the goal as replacing what it called “amateur production practices” with a “professional, robust, and scalable Architecture for State communications.”

According to the report, participants produced more than 40 pieces of content, while trainers evaluated at least 24 publications. Materials reviewed by Citizen Lab also showed Facebook and Instagram accounts and pages used in the campaign.

title: US Charges Russian Network in Alleged European Sabotage, US Murder Plot
content:
A newly unsealed U.S. federal indictment reveals that a Russian intelligence network allegedly orchestrated a targeted attack in Prague in June 2024, part of a sprawling, Kremlin-backed assassination and sabotage campaign across Europe and the United States.

The indictment’s details align directly with a known physical attack from June 2024, when a Spanish-speaking South American national was arrested for attempting to set fire to a Prague public transport bus depot. At the time, Czech Prime Minister Petr Fiala explicitly linked the incident to Moscow, stating on social media: "The unsuccessful arson attack on the buses of the Prague transport company was likely organized and financed by Russia."

Despite the U.S. charges identifying the handlers behind that attack, local law enforcement’s response remains guarded. Colonel Ondřej Moravčík, spokesman for the Czech Police Presidium, told OCCRP police are not conducting any proceedings directly related to the U.S. case and have not implemented new measures.

Spokeswoman for the Czech Interior Ministry, Ivana Nguyenová, declined to address the U.S. investigation, noting only that security services continuously monitor unusual activity.

title: UK Freezes $72-Million London Townhouse in Connection to Sanctioned Prince Group Associate
content:
British authorities have frozen a $72-million property in London in connection to an alleged associate of the Prince Group, the sanctioned Cambodian conglomerate accused of operating cyber-fraud compounds staffed in part by trafficked workers. 

Documents from the U.K. Land Registry show that a woman named Zhao Chen purchased the central London property in October 2023 for 53 million pounds ($72 million). The townhouse on a private estate in the upscale neighborhood of Belgravia features a private swimming pool and spas, according to promotional material.

British authorities placed a freeze order on the property late last month, according to the official filings obtained by Transparency International and shared with OCCRP. 

The filings show that the order was made due to Zhao Chen's association with Wu An Ming, who the U.K. has designated “an asset freeze target.” The filings do not provide information about his relationship with Zhao Chen, but OCCRP found they were married.

Official documents from the Cyprus Ministry of Interior confirm that they obtained citizenship in the Mediterranean nation together in 2018 as husband and wife.

title: Independent Journalism Is Critical For European Resilience
content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen delivered the EU’s annual state of the union address on Wednesday, calling for the robust defense of European values and warning of the dangers of cognitive warfare, foreign propaganda, and disinformation powered by viral deepfakes. 

Shaped by social media algorithms and surging AI, the integrity of Europe’s information space has become a core security and economic concern as foreign adversaries and extremists seek to paralyze democracies. Von der Leyen promised to respond by toughening sanctions enforcement and putting more funds towards promoting the rule of law. 

Europe is right to treat these issues as a high-stakes, generation-defining challenge. But there was a key omission in her speech: Independent journalism is a precondition for democratic resilience, and supporting it must remain a priority for the EU. Journalism exposes the inner workings of the threats facing our institutions, and populates our public spaces with reliable, factual, nuanced information. It is the most durable answer Europe has to the disinformation and foreign interference the President warned against. Only an informed public can make free choices.

title: How to Track Down People Who Don't Want to Be Found
content:
Whether digging into a corrupt official or trying to unmask the owner of a shady shell company, investigating a person often starts with just a handful of clues.

You may have an old phone number, a name, or a face in the background of a social media post. Taking those scattered breadcrumbs and building them into a full dossier on an individual takes a systematic approach, and is all part of a day's work for the investigative researchers at OCCRP who support journalists across the network. 

This playbook lays out the basic methods, databases, and digital tricks our team uses to track down people who don’t want to be found. No matter what kind of story you're digging into, these steps will help you safely and effectively build a profile of whoever you're looking for. 

Before diving into a digital people-search, a word of warning: setting up basic security measures is essential to protect yourself.

title: Thousands Protest in Malta After Businessman Acquitted in Journalist's Murder
content:
Outrage spilled onto the streets of the Maltese capital on Wednesday evening as demonstrators gathered at the heart of Valletta, shifting from vigils to protests to demand political accountability following the acquittal of the alleged mastermind behind the 2017 assassination of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.

For 107 consecutive months - on the 16th of every month since Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb outside her home - civil society groups held silent vigils. But the Sept. 2 acquittal of Yorgen Fenech, a prominent businessman accused of orchestrating and financing the plot, transformed that quiet grief into open defiance.

Chanting “Mafia! Mafia!” and “Injustice!”, thousands of protesters marched from the Parliament building to a memorial standing directly opposite Malta’s Law Courts to lay flowers and light candles before Caruana Galizia’s portrait. Banners carried by the crowd called for the protection of journalists and democracy, declaring: “The Trial Has Ended. Our Work Has Not” and “Impunity Ends Here.”

title: French Prosecutors Seek Up to 5 Years in Prison for Sons of Ex-Yemeni President Saleh Over Ill-Gotten Assets
content:
Two sons of late Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh could face up to five years in prison as a Paris court hears charges against them for allegedly laundering tens of millions of euros in embezzled state funds and corruption proceeds.

The trial, which opened September 7 at the Paris Criminal Court, follows a 2019 investigation launched by France's National Financial Prosecutor's Office (PNF) based on a tip-off from Swiss authorities, the PNF confirmed to OCCRP on Wednesday.

Brothers Ahmed Ali Saleh, 54, and Khaled Ali Saleh, 39, are accused of laundering proceeds from corruption and laundering embezzled public funds as part of an organized criminal group. Both men are being tried in absentia and are believed to be residing in Dubai.

Their father, Ali Abdullah Saleh, ruled Yemen for 33 years until his ouster during the Arab Spring in 2012. The former president was accused of plundering billions in state funds throughout his long tenure to enrich his family and inner circle. He was killed by Houthi rebels in 2017.

title: From Fugitive to Federal Custody: Inside the Takedown of South America’s ‘King of the South’
content:
When federal agents reached out to Sebastián Marset through his girlfriend in March 2025 to persuade him to surrender, the Uruguayan drug lord who styled himself the “King of the South” mocked them, boasting that he was "smarter than the entire D.E.A. put together."

“I’m not going to surrender,” Marset declared, according to court records. “I’ll be a criminal for the rest of my life.”

Almost a year later, heavily armed Bolivian special forces raided a residential neighborhood in Santa Cruz in the pre-dawn hours, capturing the fugitive who had evaded international law enforcement for years.

By that evening, one of the most powerful drug barons in South America’s Southern Cone - wanted by federal prosecutors for laundering millions of dollars in illicit proceeds through American banks - landed on U.S. soil in handcuffs.

Now held in a federal detention center in Virginia, Marset is mounting an aggressive legal defense. A new series of court filings has laid bare a detailed record of his global operations, missing evidence, and his own cynical view of regional law enforcement.

title: Ex-French Justice Minister Stands Trial Over Renault-Nissan Consultancy Case
content:
Criminal proceedings began Wednesday against Rachida Dati, France's former Minister of Justice and Minister of Culture, and currently the mayor of a Paris arrondissement over corruption allegations stemming from her alleged lobbying work for the Renault-Nissan car making group. 

Prosecutors accuse Dati of receiving 900,000 euros (over $1 million) between 2010 and 2012 for providing consulting services to a Dutch subsidiary of Renault-Nissan without actually performing any work, all while serving as a Member of the European Parliament and working as an attorney.

The former minister will stand trial for receiving the proceeds of abuse of authority and breach of trust, as well as for corruption and passive trading in influence committed by a person holding a public elective mandate within an international organization, the European Parliament.

She stands trial alongside co-defendant Carlos Ghosn, the former CEO of Renault-Nissan. Ghosn faces charges including abuse of corporate assets, breach of trust, corruption, and active trading in influence.

title: Instead of Helping Ukraine’s Poor, Ferrexpo’s Charitable Donations Flowed to Companies Associated With Its Then-CEO
content:
In 2017, the mining giant Ferrexpo announced it had donated more than two percent of its annual revenue to a charity based near the company’s vast iron ore mines in central Ukraine. 

This charitable spending significantly outstripped the average of its industry peers, the London Stock Exchange-listed firm highlighted in an annual report. 

Yet just one year later, questions set in. 

Auditors from Deloitte noted in Ferrexpo’s 2018 annual report that they had been unable to conclude whether the charity, named Blooming Land, had in fact spent $33.5 million of Ferrexpo’s donations on charitable ends.

Ferrexpo halted donations to the charity, which it said had been set up to “independently” coordinate the firm’s corporate social responsibility spending, and commissioned an investigation into the matter.

But the results were inconclusive: an investigating committee said only that the funds “could have been misappropriated,” and that it was unable to determine the fate of the firm’s donations.

title: Lithuanian Authorities Target Founders of Failed Cryptobank
content:
Lithuanian law enforcement authorities have formally named three co-founders of the cryptocurrency project Bankera as suspects in a criminal investigation, accusing them of siphoning off at least 45 million euro ($49 million) in investor funds following one of Europe’s largest digital token sales.

The move by Lithuania’s Financial Crime Investigation Service (FCIS) marks a major escalation in a yearlong probe stemming from investigative reporting by local news outlet 15min and OCCRP. Authorities confirmed that formal notices of suspicion were issued to the founders—Mantas Mockevičius, Vytautas Karalevičius and Justas Dobiliauskas—for the unlawful dissipation of high-value assets. All three have been requested to appear for questioning but they have reportedly left the country and apparently settled in Monaco. Their lawyer has not responded to reporter's request for comment.

title: 'Flamingo Revolution' Mounts Direct Threat to Albania's Edi Rama
content:
What began as a localized environmental campaign against a luxury resort development backed by Jared Kushner has hardened into a 100-day siege of Albania’s political center, mounting the most formidable challenge in years to the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama.

Demonstrators marched along Tirana’s main thoroughfares, rallying near local high schools to mobilize students into the movement, dubbed by organizers as the “Flamingo Revolution” as flamingos inhabit the protected Vjosa-Narta wetland ecosystem where the resort was supposed to be built. Chanting “Rama, resign” and “Your time is up,” protesters confronted security forces in the latest escalation of a campaign that has repeatedly paralyzed parts of the capital.

The unrest originally erupted over government plans to allow Kushner’s firm, Affinity Partners, to construct high-end tourism facilities on the uninhabited Sazan Island and within the protected Vjosa-Narta wetland along the Adriatic coast. While Rama framed the investment as a key catalyst for tourism and European Union integration, environmentalists fiercely opposed the privatization of pristine reserves.

title: The Son of Ljubljana’s Mayor Granted Serbian Citizenship in “National Interest”
content:
Serbian authorities granted citizenship to the son of Ljubljana’s mayor under a discreet "national interest" provision while declining to publicise the justification of its decision. The move coincides with high-value real estate purchases in the Slovenian capital by a key ally of the Serbian president, a businessman at whose Belgrade villa the mayor's son registered his official residence.

According to official records obtained by investigative news outlets Oštro and KRIK, Jure Janković - son of long-serving Ljubljana Mayor Zoran Janković - was naturalized as a Serbian citizen in November 2024. Land registry documents show that the younger Janković registered his Belgrade address at a luxury villa owned by Nikola Petrović, a powerful energy executive known widely as the "best man" and close confidant of Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić.

title: Citing Trump Crypto Fortune, US Democrats Try to Derail Bill to Regulate Digital Assets
content:
Congressional Democrats are using the sudden surge in crypto wealth accumulated by U.S. President Donald Trump as a rallying cry to defeat legislation that would create a new regulatory landscape for the digital currency industry.

The Senate is scheduled to take a procedural vote Tuesday on the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, which if passed by both legislative chambers would set new rules to govern the growing crypto sector. The procedural vote is needed for the Senate to debate the measure.

In a bid to peel off some Democrats, Republican Party leaders in Congress over the weekend incorporated ethics provisions that would prevent any U.S. president or other government officials from issuing digital assets.

“It purports to prevent conflicts of interest and corruption by the president of the United States. It is a charade. It is a sham. It should prompt a no vote by every member of the United States Senate,” said Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat.
